one_line_idea: Entropy-minimization test-time adaptation gains are specialized to synthetic corruption-style shifts and vanish or reverse on natural distribution shifts.
Test-time adaptation hyperparameters are implicitly tuned on the test distribution, making reported gains circular; shift-blind hyperparameter selection erases most of them.
Core test-time adaptation conclusions were formed on batch-normalized convolutional networks and do not transfer to layer-normalized transformer foundation models.
Under long unlabeled streams, most self-supervised test-time adaptation methods eventually collapse to trivial predictions, and collapse frequency is a hidden but decisive metric.
A frozen foundation model with a test-time nearest-neighbor or retrieval-augmented classifier matches gradient-based test-time adaptation at far lower risk.
Most of what test-time adaptation improves is calibration and decision thresholds, not representation quality, and a post-hoc output correction recovers the bulk of its accuracy gain.
Test-time adaptation methods are doing implicit label-shift estimation, and explicit unlabeled class-prior correction matches them whenever the shift includes a prior change.
Single-sample adaptation methods built on augmentation consistency mostly repackage test-time augmentation ensembling, and the learning component adds little.
No current test-time adaptation method knows when not to adapt; a simple do-no-harm gate based on stream statistics prevents most catastrophic adaptation failures.
Periodic hard reset to source weights beats sophisticated anti-forgetting machinery in continual test-time adaptation over long horizons.
Episodic reset-per-shift evaluation protocols overstate test-time adaptation practicality, and realistic recurring mixed-shift streams reverse published method rankings.
Test-time prompt tuning gains for vision-language models are mostly attributable to augmentation ensembling and confident-view selection rather than to learned prompt updates.
Matching test images to the pretraining input-statistics envelope, a trivial input-space normalization, is a stronger and safer baseline than most parameter-updating test-time adaptation.
Marginal feature-alignment objectives actively hurt adaptation when source and target label distributions differ, and popular benchmarks hide this by having nearly matched label marginals.
Given a foundation-model backbone, plain confidence-thresholded self-training beats every sophisticated alignment-based adaptation method across the standard benchmark suite.
Zero-shot vision-language models have effectively saturated office-style adaptation benchmarks, making continued method development on them uninformative.
Unsupervised model selection, not adaptation method choice, is the dominant source of variance in domain adaptation outcomes, and reported method gains are smaller than selection-induced spread.
Source data hurts more than it helps once a strong foundation initialization exists: source-free adaptation matches or beats joint source-plus-target training.
A cheap a-priori adaptability score computed from foundation-model feature geometry predicts whether unsupervised adaptation will help, do nothing, or hurt on a given domain pair.

Domain invariance is the wrong objective: methods that succeed do so through implicit class-conditional alignment, and enforcing pure marginal invariance strictly removes target-discriminative information.
In dense-prediction domain adaptation, a large share of reported gains comes from resolution, crop, and class-frequency handling rather than from distribution-alignment machinery.
Adaptation methods developed on synthetic-to-real style gaps systematically fail on real-to-real shifts such as geography and time, because the two gap types have different structure.

With foundation-model backbones, the gap between domain-generalization algorithms and empirical risk minimization shrinks to zero, making algorithm-centric generalization research empirically unmotivated in the current regime.

Invariance-penalty methods fail on vision benchmarks because the annotated environments are not causally meaningful, and with environments constructed from capture metadata the same methods start working.
Weight-averaging and flat-minima methods improve domain-generalization scores through generic variance reduction that helps in-distribution equally, not through any shift-specific mechanism.
A leakage audit of the domain-generalization literature: quantifying how much of reported progress evaporates under strictly source-only model selection.
Pretraining data diversity, not model scale, is the dominant controllable factor for out-of-domain generalization at fixed compute.
Gains from style-based augmentation on stylized benchmarks anti-correlate with performance on real geographic and temporal shifts, revealing style benchmarks as a misleading target.
Per unit of in-distribution accuracy, frozen-feature linear probes generalize across domains better than end-to-end fine-tuned models, and the gap widens with shift severity.

Compositional shift, where familiar attributes and objects appear in novel combinations, is a distinct failure axis of vision foundation models that standard domain-generalization metrics never measure.
Leave-one-domain-out evaluation has such high variance across the choice of held-out domain that most published domain-generalization comparisons are statistically undecidable.
Frozen foundation-model embeddings with classical two-sample tests detect deployment distribution shift better than dedicated learned shift detectors.
Most distribution shifts flagged by monitoring systems do not harm accuracy, and harm-calibrated detection, not shift detection, is the correct monitoring objective.
Unlabeled accuracy-estimation methods fail precisely on the shift types where monitoring needs them most, and a failure taxonomy predicts when their estimates can be trusted.
The accuracy-on-the-line phenomenon is a property of shared pretraining lineages, and it breaks for adapted, fine-tuned, or intervention-modified models, undermining its use for monitoring.
Embedding-space shift detection is dominated by low-level image statistics, masking semantic shifts; band-separated tests are needed to see what actually changed.
Anytime-valid sequential tests on foundation-model embeddings give deployment shift alarms with controlled false-alarm rates, which matters more in practice than the detection-power race.
Predicting per-sample correctness under shift is more tractable than predicting aggregate accuracy, and selective prediction transfers across shifts better than accuracy estimation does.
Rankings from out-of-distribution detection benchmarks do not predict which methods detect harmful natural shift in deployment-like monitoring, revealing a benchmark-objective mismatch.
Label-shift estimators silently return confident nonsense when class-conditional distributions also shift, and a cheap self-diagnostic can flag when their assumption is violated.

Drift root-cause attribution, assigning a detected shift to interpretable factors via counterfactual reweighting in foundation-feature space, is more valuable and more tractable than drift detection itself.
Hidden batch effects inside single-domain vision test sets shrink effective sample size so much that standard error bars in evaluation papers are systematically overconfident.

Data augmentation is an unacknowledged train-time distribution shift, and its interaction with test-time shift explains part of why augmentation-trained models respond unpredictably to deployment drift.
Dataset curation filters make benchmark test sets systematically easier than deployment data, and the curation-induced optimism is quantifiable by reconstructing the rejected data.
Deployed vision models reshape the future data they receive, and this feedback loop breaks i.i.d. evaluation in a way measurable only through simulation-based protocols.
Shuffling time-stamped datasets hides temporal drift; time-respecting splits materially change both absolute accuracy and model rankings on the same data.
Realistic dependence structure in deployment streams breaks conformal prediction coverage for vision models, and the realized coverage gap is large enough to matter operationally.
Photographer intent biases class-conditional distributions toward prototypical views, and models inherit a prototype bias that surfaces as viewpoint and context fragility under deployment shift.
A measurable share of reported distribution-shift degradation is actually annotation-standard shift, where label conventions rather than images changed between source and target.
Shared-source structure within single datasets violates i.i.d. assumptions enough that cluster-aware resampling changes benchmark conclusions, not just error bars.
Foundation-model robustness gains on shift benchmarks are largely pretraining-coverage effects, and an explicit coverage audit deflates claimed robustness to genuine novelty.
A time-travel evaluation using only imagery created after a model's data cutoff provides the first clean measurement of foundation-model robustness to genuine novelty.
Robustness loss under downstream fine-tuning is a smooth function of parameter movement from the pretrained point, giving a practical dial for the accuracy-robustness tradeoff.
Out-of-distribution performance saturates with model scale earlier than in-distribution performance, indicating that robustness is data-limited rather than capacity-limited.
Foundation models are relatively less robust to low-level sensor and compression shifts than smaller supervised models, and their celebrated robustness advantage is semantic-only.

Measured robustness differences between zero-shot and probed versions of the same backbone show that the classification head, not the representation, drives much of the foundation-model robustness story.
At matched pretraining data, contrastive, captioning, and self-supervised objectives yield similar distribution-shift robustness, showing that the objective is incidental and data is the whole story.
Robustness-intervention effects measured on small models predict their effects on foundation-scale models, enabling cheap screening before expensive integration.
Background and texture shortcut reliance survives foundation-model scale essentially unchanged; scale reduces failure frequency but not the failure mechanism.
Retrieval and classification robustness of the same vision-language model diverge under identical shifts, so single-task robustness certification is misleading for multi-use foundation models.
Instruction tuning and preference alignment of vision-language assistants degrade the distribution-shift robustness of their underlying visual competence, an unmeasured robustness tax.
Averaging weights of independently fine-tuned models recovers more of the robustness lost to fine-tuning than any specialized robust-training objective, at zero inference cost.
Benchmark domains are confounded bundles of style, content, and class-balance factors, and factorized shift benchmarks would reattribute much of what the field calls domain gap.
As in-distribution accuracy saturates, effective-robustness slopes become statistically unidentifiable, and the field needs harder in-distribution benchmarks merely to keep measuring robustness.
No robustness method Pareto-dominates across shift types, and shift-type profiles should replace single-number robustness leaderboards.

Subpopulation-shift benchmarks overstate the availability of group labels, and under realistic group-label-free conditions the reported superiority of group-robust methods over plain training shrinks or vanishes.
Adversarially-filtered hard test sets measure disagreement with the filter model rather than distribution shift, and robustness conclusions drawn from them are filter-relative artifacts.
Robustness benchmark numbers are unstable to preprocessing details at magnitudes comparable to published method gains, and a preprocessing-sensitivity audit is a missing requirement.
Caching and re-using per-condition adapters, a domain memory, beats continual gradient updating under recurring shift conditions and eliminates catastrophic forgetting by construction.
The optimal adaptation learning rate under gradual drift is a function of measurable drift speed, and an adaptive-rate law derived from it beats every fixed-rate configuration.
Long-horizon stability of online adaptation is governed by the dimensionality of the updated parameter subspace, and full-parameter online updating diverges with probability approaching one.
A divergence anchor to the frozen source model replaces stored source data in online adaptation, giving replay-level stability at zero storage and no privacy cost.
Test-time adaptation methods silently assume covariate shift, and under label-conditional drift they confidently adapt in the wrong direction, making things worse than no adaptation.
Self-supervised test-time training helps only when the auxiliary task is statistically coupled to the shift, and a computable coupling diagnostic predicts its sign of effect.
Online adaptation methods are broken by realistic non-uniform arrival processes such as class bursts, and arrival-robustness should be a first-class evaluation axis.
Under matched compute budgets, simple adaptation baselines beat sophisticated methods, and a compute-normalized leaderboard would invert much of the field's perceived ranking.
Generic distribution-divergence measures do not predict transfer performance drop across domains, while cheap hypothesis-disagreement measures do, and the field keeps reporting the wrong quantity.

Most accuracy degradation of foundation models under natural shift is captured by a two-parameter description, class-prior change plus uniform margin erosion, enabling label-free degradation forecasting.
Shift magnitude should be measured in the model's decision-relevant subspace, not in input or generic feature space, and a decision-aware shift norm predicts harm where existing measures fail.
Transferability-estimation metrics fail exactly when the probe data is shifted from deployment data, and a shift-aware correction term restores their usefulness for model selection.
Enforcing invariance to a nuisance factor provably trades away robustness to shifts correlated with that factor, and the tradeoff is measurable and large in controlled vision experiments.
Importance weighting for covariate shift, long dismissed as hopeless in high dimensions, becomes practical when density ratios are estimated in foundation-model embedding space.
Language is an adaptation surface: systematic per-domain prompt construction matches gradient-based adaptation of vision-language models at a tiny fraction of the cost and risk.

The text tower has its own distribution-shift problem: class-name register, dialect, and terminology shifts degrade vision-language classification as much as image shifts, and no benchmark measures this axis.

Under image distribution shift, vision-language assistants lean harder on language priors, so their accuracy degrades gracefully while their visual grounding collapses, and accuracy-only evaluation hides the swap.
The caption-style provenance of pretraining data determines which visual shifts a vision-language model is robust to, giving each model a predictable robustness fingerprint.
Cross-modal agreement between image and text pathways is a label-free estimator of shift harm specific to vision-language models, outperforming confidence-based estimators.
Generative vision models used as classifiers have a qualitatively different distribution-shift robustness profile than discriminative foundation models, defining an unexplored complementary paradigm.
The synthetic-to-real gap in super-resolution is dominated by unmodeled noise and compression, not by blur-kernel mismatch, so blind-kernel estimation attacks a second-order problem.
Large randomized degradation pipelines teach models the artifact statistics of the pipeline itself, and a small set of camera-measured degradations transfers better to real photos.
The composition order of degradations matters more than degradation diversity for real-world restoration transfer.
Per-image single-kernel estimation in blind SR is a mis-specified problem because real point-spread functions are spatially varying and chromatically aberrated.
Modeling degradations in the raw sensor domain and passing them through an ISP simulator transfers better than modeling degradations directly in sRGB space.
Degradation pipelines undersample the mild-degradation regime that dominates real photos, so blind models are miscalibrated toward over-restoration of nearly clean inputs.

Modern phone photos are already processed by on-device neural enhancement, so the dominant real-world degradation family is neural-network-induced, and classic degradation models are increasingly obsolete.
Many practically low-quality images were never downsampled, so framing super-resolution as inverse downsampling is a category error for a large share of use cases.
Blind-SR kernel estimates are echoes of the learned image prior rather than measurements, and they collapse on images that violate natural-image statistics.
A few minutes of per-device calibration beats universal blind restoration, because devices cluster tightly in degradation space.
A degradation-space distance between training pipeline outputs and real photos predicts real-world transfer better than benchmark scores do.
Real-world paired SR benchmarks reward slight blur because zoom-lens pair alignment errors make hedged, soft predictions optimal under full-reference metrics.
Unpaired real-world restoration methods secretly depend on the same hand-crafted degradation assumptions they claim to avoid.
Per-image test-time adaptation from internal recurrence beats adding more pretraining data for real-world restoration at foundation scale.
Blind restoration fails as a cliff, not a slope, just outside its training severity range, and the cliff location is predictable from training data alone.
A small mixture-of-experts routed by degradation archetype beats a monolithic blind model of equal total capacity on real photos.
A single user-facing fidelity-versus-enhancement dial captures most practical value of degradation estimation, making precise automatic estimation unnecessary for consumer restoration.
The blind restoration setting ignores freely available capture metadata that carries most of the degradation information the models struggle to estimate.

Restoration models fail systematically on non-photographic content because both degradation models and image priors are photo-centric, and a content-type failure taxonomy would expose this blind spot.
Analog degradations in old photos form a structurally different family from digital ones, and models trained on digital pipelines hallucinate when facing film-era artifacts.
The practically relevant perception-distortion tradeoff is per-region, not per-model, and a single global operating point is wrong for most images.
Learned perceptual metrics are gameable by artifact styles matched to their training distribution, and metric-tuned SR models exhibit a recognizable metric texture.
Human preference between faithful and hallucinated restorations reverses with viewing time and ground-truth knowledge, so time-limited studies structurally favor hallucination.
The empirical perception-distortion frontier is largely a loss mis-specification artifact, and a properly specified conditional likelihood model can dominate both endpoints simultaneously.

Replacing distortion-to-reference with consistency-to-observation as the fidelity axis makes the perception tradeoff much milder, and consistency should be the reported fidelity metric for generative restoration.
Human-preferred restorations systematically degrade machine consumption (OCR, recognition), so perceptual quality and machine quality are diverging objectives needing separate outputs.
Restoration models should output a hallucination map, and cross-seed variance of generative restorers already provides one that flags fabricated regions.
Perceived restoration quality saturates under realistic viewing conditions, and beyond a resolvable-detail threshold the field is optimizing differences invisible to users.
GAN-versus-diffusion differences in restoration quality are dominated by training data and loss weighting rather than the generative framework itself.
Face restoration homogenizes identity, drifting restored faces toward the training distribution's typical attributes, measurable as systematic embedding shift.
Restoration models should abstain on illegible text instead of fabricating legible wrong characters, and text-aware abstention is implementable without hurting non-text quality.
Late-stage sampling in diffusion-based SR is only weakly conditioned on the input, so the fine detail users see is mostly prior draw rather than evidence.
Sample diversity in stochastic restoration is misallocated: seeds vary irrelevant texture while collapsing on semantically ambiguous content where diversity actually matters.
Fixed default guidance scales in diffusion restoration are wrong for most images, and per-image guidance calibration from consistency residuals recovers substantial quality for free.
One-step distilled diffusion restorers quietly revert to GAN-like regression behavior, losing the posterior diversity that justified diffusion while keeping its reputation.
Generative restorers are unstable inverse maps: imperceptible input perturbations flip hallucinated semantic content, undermining forensic use.
Generative restorers can inject memorized training images into outputs on ambiguous inputs, and restoration needs a memorization-probe protocol like generation has.
The field needs a formal restoration-versus-reimagination boundary based on information recoverable from the observation, and most perceptual SR crosses it without disclosure.
Text-to-image foundation priors import aesthetic bias into restoration: outputs drift toward beautified renditions rather than faithful ones.
Vision-language-guided restoration converts caption errors into confident pixel hallucinations, a compounding error mode absent from caption-free restorers.
Restoration quality saturates with model scale much earlier than generation quality because the task is observation-bounded, making restoration a poor showcase for foundation-scale compute.
Universal all-in-one restoration models suffer negative transfer on hard cases, losing to per-task specialists at matched capacity despite average-metric parity.
Self-supervised foundation features are worse perceptual-loss backbones than older supervised features because SSL objectives explicitly learn invariances that a fidelity metric must not have.
Instruction-based restoration is prompt-fragile: paraphrases of the same enhancement request produce materially different outputs, and no benchmark measures this instability.

A systematic failure atlas of foundation-model restoration would show failures concentrating where the prior is strongest and the evidence weakest, inverting the intuition that strong priors help most on hard content.
In-context restoration examples act as style anchors rather than degradation evidence: shuffled or mismatched example pairs work nearly as well as correct ones.
Hallucination severity in restoration increases with the underlying generative model's training compute, making prior scale a liability metric that should be disclosed.

Repeated passes through neural processing (restoration, editing, recompression) create a compounding neural degradation family that classic degradation models cannot express, and future restorers must model it explicitly.
Standard SR ground truths are themselves degraded, imposing a hidden quality ceiling and penalizing models that exceed ground-truth quality.
Classic SR test sets are tiny and photographically dated, and method rankings would reshuffle on modern imagery, meaning part of reported progress is dataset-era artifact.
Luma-only PSNR evaluation lets SR models neglect chroma, and hidden color artifacts are widespread but unmeasured.

Silent differences in evaluation conventions (border cropping, color conversion, bit-depth handling) across SR papers are large enough to reorder nearby methods, and a conventions audit would reveal non-reproducible margins.
No-reference quality metrics actively reward hallucination in generative SR because modern fabrication artifacts lie outside their training distortion domains.
Crop-based human studies over-sample regions where hallucination looks good, and whole-image task-driven protocols would flip some perceptual-SR conclusions.
Real degradation severity is bimodal (mostly mild plus a hard tail) while benchmarks concentrate on mid-range severity, so deployment-weighted evaluation would change model choices.

Expected-distortion evaluation of stochastic restorers penalizes legitimate posterior diversity, and set-based or distributional fidelity metrics are required to compare generative restoration fairly.
Training restoration losses in gamma-encoded sRGB misweights shadow and highlight errors, and linear-light loss computation changes model behavior visibly in low light.
The field optimizes 4x magnification while deployment overwhelmingly needs mild continuous scales, and mild-scale performance is not predicted by 4x benchmark scores.

High-resolution training targets contain sensor noise that models learn to reproduce, so part of learned texture synthesis is actually noise imitation, and denoised-target training changes the perceptual character of outputs.
Real degradations vary strongly across the frame, and globally-conditioned restoration produces spatially inconsistent quality that per-region degradation conditioning fixes.
Restoration models exploit the correlation between content and degradation in real data as a shortcut, and they misrestore counterfactual images where the correlation is broken.
Tiled inference silently degrades large-image restoration through seam artifacts and context truncation, and patch-benchmark scores hide a whole-image quality gap.

Training against a single ground-truth realization teaches models false confidence at high magnification, and the one-target assumption is the root of both blur (regression) and overconfident fabrication (generation).

Eight-bit quantization of training pairs imposes an ignored information floor, causing banding-related failure modes and capping low-contrast detail recovery that higher-bit-depth training would unlock.

Restored images are almost always re-compressed downstream, and optimizing restoration jointly with expected re-compression changes what the optimal output looks like, devaluing fragile hallucinated texture.
Restoration models entangle tone and color enhancement with structural restoration, and disentangling shows part of perceived restoration quality is uncredited color grading.
Warped-frame temporal consistency metrics reward temporally stable hallucination over faithful but variable detail, making them anti-fidelity in exactly the hard cases.
The multi-frame advantage of video SR collapses on properly anti-aliased or heavily compressed footage, because models exploit temporal aliasing as their main cross-frame cue.

Codec-informed video restoration using bitstream metadata (block boundaries, motion vectors, quantization levels) beats blind pixel-space restoration at equal capacity, and discarding the bitstream is an unforced error.
Recurrent video restorers accumulate hallucination drift over long sequences, diverging from input content in ways short-clip benchmarks never measure.
Short-clip training gives recurrent video restorers an implicit state-reset bias, making their effective temporal receptive field far shorter than architecture diagrams claim.
Face-video enhancement alters lip and expression micro-motion, measurably changing perceived speech and emotion, a safety-relevant failure invisible to every current metric.
Video restoration allocates compute suboptimally across frames: temporal information saturates after a few neighbors, and reallocating compute to per-frame quality dominates at fixed budget.

Synthetic video SR benchmarks miss the coupling between motion blur, shutter time, and frame rate in real capture, and this coupling breaks synthetic-to-real transfer more than spatial degradation mismatch.
Restore-then-recognize pipelines lose to recognition models trained directly on degraded inputs, because restoration destroys machine-relevant evidence while adding human-pleasing detail.
Generative restoration invalidates images as evidence, and restoration systems for forensic contexts should emit per-region fidelity certificates grounded in observation consistency.

Natural-photo priors contaminate scientific imagery: restoration models trained on photographs inject natural-image statistics into scientific data, creating plausible artifacts that could mislead analysis.

In safety-critical imaging, hallucination concentrates on exactly the fine structures that matter most, and abstention-based restoration (enhance only what evidence supports) is the correct product for these domains.

Restoration-as-decoder compression schemes (send low quality, restore at receiver) are evaluated with perceptual metrics that hide semantic drift, and round-trip semantic audits would cap their claimed bitrate savings.

For machine consumption, restoring feature embeddings directly beats restoring pixels first: pixel space is a human-oriented bottleneck that wastes capacity on visually pleasing but task-irrelevant detail.
Face enhancement shifts identity-verification scores asymmetrically across demographic groups, so restoration can silently change biometric outcomes with disparate impact.

Most claimed architecture gains in SR are training-recipe gains: under matched modern recipes, a decade of architectural innovations compresses into a much smaller quality spread than the literature implies.
SR models are not scale-consistent (twice 2x differs from once 4x), and enforcing scale-composition consistency at training improves generalization to unseen scales for free.
Small-crop training biases SR models against global structure: long edges, vanishing lines, and large-scale gradients are reconstructed with systematic errors that large-context training fixes.
SR models get amplitude spectra roughly right but phase systematically wrong, and phase error is the better predictor of perceived structural artifacts, motivating phase-aware losses.
Restoration data scaling hits diminishing returns quickly on content diversity but not on degradation diversity, so data budgets should buy degradations, not images.
SR models collapse rare textures onto common ones: outputs re-render unusual materials as the nearest frequent texture family, a measurable prior-collapse effect invisible to aggregate metrics.
Blind training over mixed severities teaches models a severity-averaged inverse that is wrong for every severity, and cheap explicit severity conditioning dominates blind averaging.
Overparameterized SR models memorize training patches retrievably: nearest-neighbor probes on outputs would reveal patch-level copying, qualifying texture-generalization claims.
Iterative refinement helps sampling, not restoration: at matched compute, single-pass fidelity models match multi-step ones, and iteration only pays when the goal is drawing from a distribution.
Test-time geometric self-ensembling gains expose a fixable equivariance defect: equivariance-regularized training recovers the ensemble's benefit in a single pass.

The semantically strongest layer/timestep for diffusion-feature extraction is set by signal-to-noise ratio, not raw timestep index, and therefore transfers across models and noise schedules once re-parameterized in SNR.
Dense correspondence ability in diffusion features lives in self-attention key/query geometry, not in convolutional value pathways, and the two can be dissociated by targeted feature surgery.

v-prediction and x0-prediction models yield markedly better high-noise semantic features than epsilon-prediction models of matched quality, because their outputs remain image-like where epsilon targets are nearly pure noise.

Diffusion features encode intrinsic scene properties (albedo, shading, material gloss) more linearly than contrastive or masked-image features, because generation requires photometric competence that discriminative objectives can discard.

Depth structure readable from image-diffusion features reflects genuinely 3D-consistent knowledge rather than 2D shading heuristics, testable by randomizing photometric cues and checking cross-view probe consistency.

Conditional denoisers queried with a null prompt produce semantically richer features than genuinely unconditional models of matched scale, because text conditioning during training organizes the internal representation even when unused at inference.

Multi-timestep diffusion feature ensembles are mostly redundant: the timestep-feature stack has low effective rank, and a single well-chosen timestep plus a linear map recovers nearly all probe performance.

Diffusion transformers develop high-norm 'register-like' tokens analogous to those in supervised ViTs, and these tokens store global photometric/style state whose deletion selectively breaks style while sparing layout.

Perception heads trained on one diffusion backbone transfer to a different diffusion backbone through a single linear adapter, indicating a shared 'generative representation geometry' across independently trained models.

Generative pretraining specifically resolves symmetric-part ambiguity in semantic correspondence (left/right paws, wheels), predicting a large margin over discriminative features exactly on symmetry-confusable pairs and near-parity elsewhere.

Generative depth estimators fine-tuned from image diffusion models inherit a photometric prior that fails predictably on non-photorealistic inputs, locating the boundary of the 'repurpose a generator' recipe.

Image generators know occluded shape: diffusion features support amodal (completed-shape) segmentation probes far above discriminative features, because generation requires representing whole objects before occlusion.

Diffusion-classifier accuracy is bottlenecked by noise-sample variance rather than model knowledge, so paired-noise variance reduction closes most of the gap to discriminative readouts at a fraction of the usual inference cost.

Cross-attention localization in text-to-image models collapses selectively for relational prompts: attention maps localize single objects well but misassign attributes in two-object scenes at a rate predictable from token co-occurrence statistics.
Occlusion ordering (which object is in front) is linearly decodable from diffusion self-attention geometry without any depth supervision, and more accurately than from discriminative features.

Diffusion features degrade more gracefully under common corruptions than discriminative features, with a measurable crossover severity beyond which the denoising-adjacent pretraining advantage dominates.

Structured inpainting is a scene-understanding test: masking context-critical regions and scoring semantic plausibility of completions yields a graded measure of what a generator understands about scenes, orthogonal to image-quality scores.

Single-image diffusion features carry motion affordances: a linear probe predicts the plausible optical-flow direction field of a static frame, revealing implicit dynamics knowledge in image-only generators.

A one-step distilled diffusion model retains most of the parent's dense-perception feature quality at 1/20th the extraction cost, making diffusion backbones cost-competitive with discriminative ViTs for the first time.

Classifier-free guidance sharpens the output distribution with a lawful, measurable exponent: embedding-space sample variance shrinks as a power law in guidance scale, with mode-dropping onset at a critical scale predictable from conditional/unconditional score divergence.
CFG's benefit is confined to a narrow mid-trajectory SNR window, and its artifacts (oversaturation, waxy textures) are produced almost entirely by applying guidance outside that window at low noise.

The null-prompt baseline in CFG is the wrong anchor: replacing the empty-string unconditional branch with a learned corpus-mean prompt embedding yields equal alignment at lower guidance scales with fewer artifacts.

Negative prompts and positive guidance are mechanistically asymmetric: negation via score subtraction removes appearance features but cannot remove relational or compositional content, predicting a measurable class of un-negatable concepts.

Guidance direction transfers across model scale: the conditional-minus-unconditional score direction computed by a small cheap model can steer a large model's sampling with most of the alignment benefit at a fraction of the compute.

High guidance scales amplify verbatim training-set recall: for duplication-prone prompts, extraction rates rise superlinearly with guidance scale because guidance sharpens toward memorized attractors.

Per-prompt optimal guidance scale is predictable from prompt statistics alone (token rarity, length, specificity), enabling a trained scale-predictor that beats any fixed global scale on the alignment-diversity Pareto front.

Cross-model CFG (conditional branch from model A, unconditional from model B) works if and only if the two models' score fields agree up to an affine map, giving an operational compatibility test for mixing generative models.

Perceptual guidance strength is what saturates, not information: past a modest scale, extra guidance stops adding text-relevant image content and only shifts global statistics, measurable as a plateau in mutual-information proxies between prompt tokens and image regions.

DDIM inversion error is spectrally lawful: reconstruction error concentrates where local high-frequency energy is high, so a cheap spectral map of an image predicts where subsequent edits will fail before any editing is attempted.

Inversion failure under classifier-free guidance is a per-timestep bias, not noise: the error grows systematically with guidance scale, and null-text-style fixes work precisely because they absorb this bias term, which can be measured and corrected directly.

Iterated invert-edit cycles converge to model-typical attractor images: identity drifts toward the generator's mean style at a measurable geometric rate, giving a quantitative 'regression to the generative mean' law for sequential editing.

The inversion-error gap between model-generated and real photographs of matched content is a quantitative measure of the generator's manifold mismatch, usable as a model-diagnostic that tracks training data coverage.

No attention-based 'local' editor is actually local: every mainstream inversion-editing method leaks measurable background change, with a floor that current architectures cannot cross, quantified by a background-drift budget protocol.

Invertibility collapses discontinuously as sampling steps shrink: below a critical step count the inversion round-trip error jumps rather than degrades smoothly, defining a phase boundary for edit-capable fast sampling.

Stochastic strength in SDEdit-style editing has a universal sweet spot in SNR terms: the structure-preservation versus realism crossover happens at a similar effective noise level across domains and models, collapsing a per-use hyperparameter to a constant.

Inverted latents carry a prompt fingerprint: inverting an image under the wrong caption embeds recoverable traces of that caption, biasing all downstream edits in measurable, caption-specific directions.

Round-trip consistency (apply an edit, then apply its inverse instruction) is a label-free capability measure for instruction editors, and current editors will fail it at rates that single-edit benchmarks completely hide.

Verbatim memorization versus duplication count follows a sharp sigmoidal threshold, and the threshold location shifts predictably with model capacity, yielding a quantitative memorization law usable for dataset dedup policy.

Text keys, not image copies, gate verbatim recall in text-to-image models: perturbing the prompt away from the memorized caption collapses extraction rates even for heavily duplicated images, enabling inference-time mitigation without retraining.

Memorized items sit in measurably sharper score-field attractors: reverse trajectories initialized in a neighborhood converge to memorized images faster and from a wider basin than to novel generations, giving a geometric signature of memorization.

Prompt-keyed memorization is stored in a localizable sliver of weights (dominantly cross-attention K/V): ablating under 1% of parameters removes specific memorized items with negligible global quality loss, enabling surgical unlearning.

Memorized generations commit early: their trajectories lock onto the final output at higher noise levels than novel generations, so commitment time is a mechanistic covariate of memorization measurable without reference to training data.

Generators memorize compositions far more than pixels: layout-level templates from training data recur in generations at rates vastly exceeding verbatim copying, constituting a second, unmeasured tier of memorization.

Personalization fine-tuning (LoRA/DreamBooth-style) memorizes its few training images at rates orders of magnitude above pretraining memorization, with leakage growing superlinearly in fine-tuning steps, making 'private personalization' claims measurable and mostly false.

Standard augmentations suppress pixel-tier memorization but leave layout-tier memorization intact, so the field's main training mitigation fixes the audited symptom while preserving the unaudited one.

Removing memorized attractors improves the model elsewhere: surgical unlearning of verbatim items increases sample diversity and prompt fidelity in the semantic neighborhood of the removed content, showing memorization actively harms nearby generalization.

Semantic layout is decided in a narrow early window of the reverse trajectory: swapping conditioning or noise mid-trajectory localizes a universal 'decision point' in SNR units beyond which content is frozen and only appearance changes.
